Egypt is high-risk for trans visitors — with a directly documented study on the treatment of queer foreigners by Egyptian authorities ("Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here," Cairo 52, 12 incidents 2018-2022). Same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalised, but authorities use "debauchery" and cybercrime laws (six months + fine for "violation of social and family values") to arrest and prosecute — and courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation under the cybercrime law.

Police hunt LGBT people on dating apps (BBC Grindr entrapment) and subject arrestees to coerced anal examinations. Gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited. The Ministry of Interior is closing a loophole that allowed limited legal gender recognition. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity in its 2025 Universal Periodic Review. The authorities' approach is described as "not only to criminalize LGBTQ+ identities but also to erase them from society and public life."

Egypt has no death penalty for same-sex (unlike Uganda/Nigeria's death penalties), no documented trans-specific tourist killing, and the statutory penalty is six months + fine (not 14 years or life) — but the systematic police entrapment, foreigner-targeting, coerced anal exams, and healthcare prohibition make the practical risk severe.
EGY.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (Sinai), political instability, and general crime affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

PER.name: Peru
PER.summary:
Peru is elevated-risk with a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence against trans people, but no criminalisation of trans identity and an unprecedented 17-year conviction for police torture of a trans woman. Congress approved (February-April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated axis-C restriction comparable to US state bans or the UK EHRC code. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 TLGBI people were assassinated (trans women most affected). In the Azul Rojas Marín case, three police officers were sentenced to 17 years for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman (December 2025) — an unprecedented conviction for Peru and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. A presidential decree briefly classified trans identity as a "mental disorder" (May 2024), but was walked back after massive protests.

Legal gender recognition exists via the courts but is expensive, complicated, and can take years. No self-ID law has been passed (blocked by conservative majorities since 2016). No same-sex marriage. For a visitor: no border friction, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure when using public facilities.
PER.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (theft, robbery) and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

URY.name: Uruguay
URY.summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, self-ID legal gender recognition, and Montevideo is welcoming. Uruguay's comprehensive legal framework (self-ID, reparation pension, state employment quota, protected bathrooms, stable progressive government, 'safest in LatAm') places it above Chile and Argentina, around the Japan/Taiwan level — above the UK (which has an in-force daily bathroom code, strip-search policies, and men's-prison placement post-Supreme-Court) by approximately 0.10, reflecting the five axes on which Uruguay is systematically better (bathrooms protected, no strip-search, no men's-prison rollback, self-ID vs court-GRC, stable vs deteriorating climate).
URY.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is very low; no trans-specific travel advisory.

QAT.name: Qatar
QAT.summary:
Qatar is Do Not Travel for trans visitors, with the most severe documented police practice in the Gulf. Human Rights Watch interviewed four transgender women arrested by the Preventive Security Department between 2019 and 2022 based solely on their gender expression in public places. One was arrested for wearing makeup — officers made her wipe it off, used the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her, and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All described sexual harassment in custody, forced phone-unlocking to identify other LGBT people, and mandatory conversion-therapy sessions as a condition of release. Detention was in an underground prison in Doha; one woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and physical detransition (forced breast-tissue removal) was reported.

No statute has been repealed: trans people are arrested for "impersonating the opposite gender" and "violating public morality" under community-protection laws allowing up to 6 months' detention without charge or trial. Arrests continued even during the 2022 World Cup under international scrutiny.

Unlike Kuwait (statute repealed, courts awarding compensation) or Bahrain (rare enforcement), Qatar's targeting of gender expression is systematic, current, and unreformed — placing it below both despite their shared Gulf context.
QAT.outOfScopeNotes: Migrant-worker abuses, kafala labour system, and general human-rights concerns affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

KWT.name: Kuwait
KWT.summary:
Kuwait is High Risk — the least hostile of the Gulf states, but not safe. In 2007, Article 198 of the Penal Code criminalised "imitating the opposite sex in any way" (up to 1 year in jail); within two weeks at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, coffee shops, and taxis, three were beaten (one into unconsciousness), and heads were shaved as punishment. HRW's 2012 report "They Hunt Us Down for Fun" documented police violence against trans women under this law.

However, in February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck down Article 198 as unconstitutional — the only Gulf state to repeal its cross-dressing statute. The repeal has teeth: a cisgender woman arrested over a short haircut won 4,000 KWD in compensation, with the Court of Cassation ruling police had arrested her "without justification." Being visibly trans is no longer a crime in Kuwait.

But the repeal is incomplete in practice: HRW reports transgender people "continue to face threats and harassment," and in December 2022 security forces carried out mass deportations of LGBT people under "security" measures. For a trans traveler: no criminal exposure for gender expression itself, courts now provide recourse, but police harassment and deportation risk remain real, and same-sex conduct (a situational factor for trans visitors with partners) remains criminalised at up to 7 years.
KWT.outOfScopeNotes: Migrant-worker labour conditions affect all foreign workers; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

BHR.name: Bahrain
BHR.summary:
Bahrain is Do Not Travel, but with the thinnest active-enforcement record in the Gulf. Uniquely among Gulf states, same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1976, and there is no statute criminalising transgender expression. The UK foreign office notes "arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare."

However, broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions are used against gender and sexual minorities — penalties include imprisonment, fines, and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a Manama hotel discotheque on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A Brazilian trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite a female passport marker. In 2023 a court rejected a trans man's recognition application citing Islamic Sharia, and in February 2024 the lower house of parliament adopted a bill to criminalise "acts of deviance" — a deteriorating trajectory.

For a visitor: the legal exposure is real but enforcement is sporadic; the modal risk is indecency arrest followed by deportation rather than imprisonment. Bahrain scores above Qatar, Oman, and the UAE because it lacks both a codified gender-expression statute and a documented pattern of systematic targeting.
BHR.outOfScopeNotes: Political repression, restrictions on free expression, and labour concerns affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

OMN.name: Oman
OMN.summary:
Oman is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — and uniquely in the Gulf, combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveler abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, extending to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the Royal Oman Police publicly announced arresting transgender women in Salalah after private-party photos circulated on social media; HRW documented arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travelers: in February 2024, Nin Kala, an Indian non-binary model and designer arriving at Muscat airport on a tourist visa, was pulled aside while their friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. Kala warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these Gulf countries."

Oman scores below Qatar because it adds a codified, enforced gender-expression statute and a documented airport outing of an actual trans traveler; it stays above Saudi Arabia only because penalties are lower and no custodial death is documented.
OMN.outOfScopeNotes: Political restrictions and labour conditions affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

BGR.name: Bulgaria
BGR.summary:
Bulgaria is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — an EU member with no traveler-facing restrictions, but one of the EU's most hostile social climates. There is no bathroom law, no border friction for foreign passports, and no criminalisation of gender expression. The European Court of Justice is actively hearing the Shipov case on Bulgaria's refusal to issue ID matching lived gender, and EU free-movement law provides a legal backstop.

The concerns are climate rather than traveler law: the Supreme Court of Cassation ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible (gender an "unchangeable biological factor"), parliament passed a Russia-style law banning "propaganda" of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools (August 2024), and the EU's FRA survey finds 75% of LGBTIQ people in Bulgaria avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault — both far above EU averages. Hate speech by politicians is routine.

For a visitor: document mismatch carries no legal penalty, police do not target trans expression, and Sofia has a small but visible scene. The risk is street hostility if read as trans — verbal harassment is common, physical assault possible but not systematic. Bulgaria scores below Romania (0.67, no propaganda law, less hostile FRA numbers) and level with Serbia (0.64, similar climate, no EU backstop but no propaganda law either).
BGR.outOfScopeNotes: The LGR ban and propaganda law are resident-facing; they signal climate but do not directly restrict a foreign passport holder. Roma minority issues and asylum-system abuses are out of scope.

SVK.name: Slovakia
SVK.summary:
Slovakia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. There are no traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues, EU free movement, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events.

The climate is the concern. In October 2022, a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside Tepláreň, a Bratislava LGBT bar — classified as Slovakia's first modern terrorist attack. The state responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding: parliament advanced a bill to make legal gender recognition impossible (genetic-test-only basis), and constitutional amendments declaring gender immutable have been proposed. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in Bratislava.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, but elevated risk of street hostility and a political trajectory moving against trans recognition. Slovakia scores above Hungary (0.68 — LGR already banned there plus a propaganda law in force), below Poland (0.72 — no terrorist attack and larger protective infrastructure), and well below Czechia (0.74).
SVK.outOfScopeNotes: The LGR-ban bill and constitutional gender amendments are resident-facing climate signals. Roma discrimination is out of scope.

BLR.name: Belarus
BLR.summary:
Belarus is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. In 2024 the authorities escalated from hostility to active persecution: a Culture Ministry decree reclassified transgender identity itself — "the desire to live and be seen by others as a person of an opposite sex" — as pornography, punishable by up to four years in prison. In September 2024 a wave of arrests targeted the community: TG House Belarus documented over 15 LGBTQ+ people detained, including at least eight transgender people, several arrested for merely subscribing to "extremist" resources online.

Detained trans people were beaten and forced to record humiliating "confession videos" circulated on pro-government channels. ODIHR's 2024 reporting notes the majority of bias incidents in Belarus targeted trans people, including "physical assaults, threats, abductions, humiliation, and coerced confessions related to their gender identity by law enforcement officers." State media runs systematic dehumanising propaganda.

Gender transition technically remains legal, but the 2024 pornography decree means a discoverable online presence or simply living visibly as trans can be prosecuted. For a visitor: no documented trans-tourist case yet, but police actively hunt trans people, any visible gender nonconformity risks detention, and foreign nationals receive no protection. Belarus scores just above Russia (0.12 — nationwide "extremist movement" designation and LGR ban) and below Uganda (0.17).
BLR.outOfScopeNotes: General political repression and the post-2020 protest crackdown affect everyone; the score reflects trans-specific risk.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.summary:
Ukraine is Reduced Risk for trans visitors, with the caveat that this scores trans-specific risk, not the obvious general risks of an active war zone. Ukraine criminalises nothing about being trans; legal gender recognition exists (medicalised — a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation under the 2016 protocol), and a resilient civil society (Gender Stream, Insight) operates openly. Kyiv hosted a three-day Trans Forum in June 2026 even during the war.

Trans-specific frictions exist but mostly affect residents, not visitors: trans women with male passports cannot leave the country under martial law (conscription), and wartime document checks can out people. A foreign visitor's passport is not subject to mobilisation rules, so border crossing is governed by standard wartime entry rules. There is no SOGI-specific hate-crime law, societal attitudes lag EU averages, and the healthcare system is war-disrupted (hormone shortages, diagnostic corruption reported).

Ukraine scores far above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) — no criminalisation, no state persecution, functioning NGOs — and below Serbia (0.64) and Moldova (0.65), reflecting wartime institutional strain and weaker legal protections rather than active hostility.
UKR.outOfScopeNotes: General war risks (missile strikes, infrastructure, mobilisation) apply to all travelers and are out of scope for the trans-specific score. Trans residents' draft exposure is noted as context but does not govern the visitor score.

MDA.name: Moldova
MDA.summary:
Moldova is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — the best-protected of the former-Soviet states outside the Baltics. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity, and Chisinau Pride marches through the city centre under police protection. Moldova is on the EU accession path, driving continued legal alignment.

Counterweights: there is still no accessible legal gender recognition (a medicalised process exists on paper but Genderdoc-M reports it is not functional in practice), the Orthodox Church and major politicians (including Chisinau's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements, and the breakaway Russian-controlled region of Transnistria has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travelers should treat Transnistria as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

Moldova scores below Romania (0.67 — functional LGR, EU member longer) and above Serbia (0.64 — comparable climate but Moldova's 2022 SOGI hate-crime law and EU-candidate trajectory give it the edge) and Ukraine (0.62 — war strain).
MDA.outOfScopeNotes: Transnistria is scored as part of Moldova de jure but travelers should treat it separately: Russian-controlled, anti-LGBT propaganda law, no consular access. General poverty and corruption affect all travelers.

LUX.name: Luxembourg
LUX.summary:
Luxembourg is Low Risk — one of Europe's strongest trans jurisdictions. Legal gender recognition by self-determination since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018), with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body (CET) handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (Schengen), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression/sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law.

Pairwise: level with Belgium (0.89, also self-determination LGR), below Iceland/Malta (0.95/0.94, broader coverage incl. expression and intersex protections), above the Netherlands (0.88, no self-ID LGR).

AND.name: Andorra
AND.summary:
Andorra is Low Risk for trans visitors. The 2022 Law of the Person and Family modernised the legal framework (unified civil marriage, and legal gender recognition provisions); the Ministry of Equality now obliges all companies to maintain sexual and gender-based harassment protocols. ILGA-Europe records only three bias-motivated incidents in the most recent annual review — a tiny absolute number reflecting a small, safe, tourism-dependent country.

No traveler-facing concerns: no bathroom laws, no border issues (open border with Spain/France, though outside Schengen there are no document-gender checks), high social tolerance in practice despite a conservative Catholic history. Gaps: anti-discrimination coverage of gender identity is recent and shallower than Spain's; hate-crime law is generic rather than SOGI-specific.

Pairwise: level with Germany (0.83), below Spain (0.90 — Ley Trans, comprehensive statute), above Italy (0.76 — no LGR self-determination, political hostility).
AND.outOfScopeNotes: Church influence on family law is resident-facing.

MCO.name: Monaco
MCO.summary:
Monaco is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. There is no functioning legal gender recognition process (ILGA-Europe lists Monaco among states without one), but that is a resident-facing gap: a visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever. Monaco is a tiny, heavily-policed, very low-crime tourist enclave embedded in France; street violence of any kind is rare.

No bathroom laws, no border friction (entry via France, Schengen rules), no documented anti-trans incidents. The score reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness (no LGR, limited explicit trans protections).

Pairwise: level with Slovenia (0.78), below France (0.82 — functional LGR), above Italy (0.76 — active political hostility Monaco lacks).
MCO.outOfScopeNotes: Family-law gaps (no marriage equality, cohabitation contracts only) are resident-facing.

SMR.name: San Marino
SMR.summary:
San Marino is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. ILGA-Europe lists San Marino among states with no functioning legal gender recognition process (resident-facing gap only). There is no criminalisation, no bathroom law, no border friction (open border with Italy), and no documented pattern of anti-trans violence in this tiny, tourism-dependent republic surrounded by Italy.

The score reflects very high de facto safety combined with minimal explicit legal infrastructure for trans people.

Pairwise: just below Monaco (0.78 — Monaco has explicit SOGI hate-crime law), just above Italy (0.76 — Italy has LGR but active political hostility and higher documented violence).

LIE.name: Liechtenstein
LIE.summary:
Liechtenstein is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Same-sex relations are legal and discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned, but gender identity, gender expression, and sex characteristics are not included in any anti-discrimination legislation, and there is no legal gender recognition law. These are resident-facing gaps: a visitor faces no legal exposure.

Liechtenstein is a very small, very low-crime Alpine country closely integrated with Switzerland; there is no documented pattern of anti-trans violence, no bathroom law, and no border friction (Schengen via Switzerland/Austria). Social attitudes are conservative but not mobilised-hostile.

Pairwise: level with Italy (0.76), below Switzerland (0.85 — LGR by self-declaration since 2022), above Greece (0.75 — Greece has self-ID but more documented street hostility).
LIE.outOfScopeNotes: Anti-discrimination and LGR gaps are resident-facing.

VAT.name: Vatican City
VAT.summary:
Vatican City is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — and an unusual case: it is a 0.49 km² tourist enclave (museums, basilica, square) with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathrooms inspections, no morality police, and the Swiss Guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile: the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and there is obviously no legal recognition or protection of any kind. But this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism — the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

Pairwise: level with Greece (0.75), below Italy (0.76 — actual jurisdiction with LGR and hate-crime law). Visitors sleep, eat, and transit in Italy; the Vatican score reflects the enclave experience only.
VAT.outOfScopeNotes: Doctrinal positions are climate signals; Vatican employment and canon-law matters are resident-facing.

CYP.name: Cyprus
CYP.summary:
Cyprus is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. The legal framework is mid-transition: public incitement to hatred based on gender identity is a criminal offence (2015), and gender identity is an aggravating factor in hate crime (2017). A legal gender recognition bill (self-determination basis) was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and is pending in parliament; until it passes, LGR requires surgery under the 2002 Civil Registry Law — a resident-facing gap.

No traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues (EU member), tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to diverse visitors. Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the non-discrimination framework, and the divided island matters: the northern part (de facto Turkish-controlled) has its own LGR regime requiring surgical proof, weaker protections, and less documentation — travelers should treat the north as closer to Turkey's risk profile.

Pairwise: level with Czechia (0.74) and Chile (0.74), below Greece (0.75 — self-ID LGR in force since 2017), above Israel (0.69).
CYP.outOfScopeNotes: The north/south division and pending LGR bill are noted; LGR requirements are resident-facing.

KHM.name: Cambodia
KHM.summary:
Cambodia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: the Cambodian Centre for Human Rights documents “shocking” harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported Siem Reap police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

Pairwise: below Vietnam (0.63 — LGR legislation progressing, stronger state capacity), above India (0.58). For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially.
KHM.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and discrimination-law gaps are resident-facing.

NPL.name: Nepal
NPL.summary:
Nepal is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — South Asia's most legally recognising country. The Supreme Court has protected gender identity since the landmark 2007 Sunil Babu Pant decision; a third-gender “O” category exists on documents by self-identification; and in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled (Rukshana Kapali case) that a trans woman must be recognised as female without medical verification. Nothing is criminalised, and Kathmandu has an established activist scene (Blue Diamond Society, founded 2001).

The gap between doctrine and practice is large: HRW documents (“We Have to Beg So Many People,” 2024) that implementation is piecemeal and humiliating, and trans people in provinces like Madhesh face physical and sexual harassment in public spaces with little police protection. These burdens fall overwhelmingly on residents navigating citizenship documents — a visitor with a foreign passport faces none of the bureaucratic gauntlet.

Pairwise: above Cambodia (0.61 — no judicial recognition culture), tied with Serbia (0.64 — different profiles: Nepal has stronger courts, Serbia stronger public order); below Romania (0.67). For a visitor: no legal exposure, tolerant tourist areas, but expect stares and possible harassment if visibly trans outside Kathmandu/Pokhara bubbles.
NPL.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation barriers are resident-facing; citizenship-law discrimination does not affect visitors.

LKA.name: Sri Lanka
LKA.summary:
Sri Lanka is High Risk for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

Pairwise: above Malaysia (0.28 — adds state-level Sharia “posing” laws with caning) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts and civil society). The police-as-perpetrator documentation keeps Sri Lanka in High Risk rather than Elevated.
LKA.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; LGR circular limits are resident-facing.

MNG.name: Mongolia
MNG.summary:
Mongolia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and SOGI was added to the hate-crime provisions of the Criminal Code in 2015. Legal gender recognition exists via a medicalised process, and Ulaanbaatar has an organised community (LGBT Centre) that successfully lobbied for these protections.

Counterweights: protections are fragmented (no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering all areas), the LGBT Centre has documented periods of elevated hate speech and assaults — including attacks on its own staff — and social acceptance outside the capital is low. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; the realistic risk is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside central Ulaanbaatar.

Pairwise: level with Ukraine (0.62 — different profiles: Mongolia has a SOGI hate-crime law but thinner civil society; Ukraine has war strain), below Vietnam (0.63), above Cambodia (0.61).
MNG.outOfScopeNotes: Comprehensive anti-discrimination gaps and medicalised LGR are resident-facing.

MMR.name: Myanmar
MMR.summary:
Myanmar is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Section 377 of the Penal Code criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use “shadow laws” — notably Section 30(d) of the Rangoon Police Act, allowing detention of anyone who cannot “satisfactorily account” for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: the National Unity Government documented 17 LGBT people killed by mid-2022, and rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities, with the 2024 Conscription Law falling brutally on queer people.

In 2025 the junta banned seven books for LGBTQ+ content as “obscene.” There is no legal gender recognition, no protection of any kind, and no institutional recourse — police and military are the primary predators. Resistance-controlled areas are nominally friendlier but are active war zones.

Pairwise: above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) only because Myanmar's persecution, while lethal, is part of generalised wartime violence rather than a codified anti-trans machine; below Uganda (0.17). For a visitor: any visible gender nonconformity risks detention under police-act powers, with torture documented in custody; the general security collapse compounds everything.
MMR.outOfScopeNotes: General civil-war risks affect all travelers and are out of scope; the score reflects trans-specific persecution by the junta.

CUB.name: Cuba
CUB.summary:
Cuba is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — one of Latin America's most legally transformed countries. The 2019 Constitution bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the 2022 Family Code (66.87% referendum approval) overhauled family law; and trans people can change legal gender — the July 2025 civil-registry reform further eliminated bureaucratic hurdles for name changes. CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme, and Havana has a visible, state-tolerated trans community.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific: Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, the economic crisis has degraded healthcare (hormone availability is unreliable), and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people as trans — the historical UMAP camps era is long past and officially repudiated — but there is also no independent recourse if something goes wrong.

Pairwise: below Argentina (0.73 — democracy, independent NGOs, stronger recourse) and above Lithuania (0.66) and Vietnam (0.63 — Cuba's constitutional GI protection and official trans programme edge it). For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression or documents; low street-hostility in tourist areas; the risk is the general absence of rule-of-law recourse.
CUB.outOfScopeNotes: Political repression, shortages, and detention powers affect all travelers; LGR mechanics are resident-facing.

ECU.name: Ecuador
ECU.summary:
Ecuador is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — a country whose legal framework is now among Latin America's strongest while its streets are among the region's most dangerous. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016; the 2024 Organic Law reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the ID card directly through the Civil Registry (one time, no surgery); and in 2024-25 Constitutional Court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the Assembly for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: Runa Sipiy documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023, with inadequate state response, and the “internal armed conflict” against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024 — two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks. Quito and Guayaquil carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis.

Pairwise: above Colombia (0.55 — Ecuador's LGR is now simpler) and below India (0.58 — comparable; Ecuador has far better law, India lower targeted-murder rate). For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in South America right now.
ECU.outOfScopeNotes: The general security emergency affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific legal/violence balance.

JAM.name: Jamaica
JAM.summary:
Jamaica is High Risk for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

Pairwise: above Malaysia (0.28 — adds Sharia caning statutes) and below Sri Lanka (0.33 — police-as-perpetrator but less mob-killing culture). Jamaica's mob-violence pattern plus failed investigation of the Dwayne Jones killing keeps it in High Risk.
JAM.outOfScopeNotes: The buggery law is a situational/climate factor; resort vs. non-resort risk differs sharply.

TTO.name: Trinidad and Tobago
TTO.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

Pairwise: above Kenya (0.38 — TTO decriminalised via courts; Kenya retains criminalisation) and below Turkey (0.47). For a visitor: no legal exposure for being trans, functioning courts, but meaningful outing-violence and dating-app-ambush risk, with police more likely to warn than protect.
TTO.outOfScopeNotes: Decriminalisation status and reform rejections are climate/legal context; no trans-specific statute exists.

GHA.name: Ghana
GHA.summary:
Ghana is High Risk for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” President Akufo-Addo refused to assent pending legal challenges, the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. Accra has a resilient underground community (LGBT+ Rights Ghana — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.

Pairwise: above Nigeria (0.19 — SSMPA in force with mob lynching culture) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts). Ghana's near-passage of an identity-criminalising bill is what separates it from Elevated band: the legal floor is currently the old 3-year statute, but the demonstrated legislative intent is far harsher.
GHA.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 bill never became law (lapsed unassented); its significance is climate/trajectory.

MAR.name: Morocco
MAR.summary:
Morocco is High Risk for trans visitors. Article 489 criminalises same-sex “indecent acts” (6 months–3 years), and Cairo 52 documents that trans people face de-facto criminalisation under Article 498 morality provisions — arrests based on gender-expression discrepancies and forced outing. The 2026 Cairo 52 report “A Web of Violence” describes a legal-medical-social system of erasure for trans people, including a de facto prohibition on transition care.

Visitor-relevant cases exist: in 2024, Brazilian influencer Liziane Gutierrez was arrested in Marrakesh, accused by police of being transgender, and alleges she was forced to show her genitals — she spent a month in jail. In 2019, Marrakesh police filmed and humiliated a cross-dressing man after a traffic accident, leaking the video online. There is no LGR framework and police have wide discretion; tourist areas (Marrakesh, Agadir) are more tolerant in practice but the legal exposure is constant.

Pairwise: level with Indonesia (0.25) and Pakistan (0.26), above Egypt (0.22 — adds systematic entrapment machinery), below Malaysia (0.28). The Gutierrez case demonstrates that even a cisgender visitor suspected of being trans can face genital inspection and jail.
MAR.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; the 2024 Gutierrez arrest was officially for filming a policeman — the trans-suspicion genital inspection is her allegation, disputed by Morocco.

DZA.name: Algeria
DZA.summary:
Algeria is High Risk for trans visitors. Gender transition is not explicitly criminalised, but Cairo 52 documents that it is effectively criminalised through Penal Code Articles 333, 338, and 333 bis (indecency provisions), and NGOs have documented arrests of LGBT+ people under these articles. Same-sex activity itself carries up to 2 years under Article 338. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and no visible community infrastructure — activism operates almost entirely underground.

Unlike Tunisia or Morocco, Algeria lacks even a documented trans-visitor incident — partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access. The legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor (indecency arrest) is real but the enforcement pattern is thinner than Egypt's entrapment machinery or Tunisia's 2024-25 arrest wave.

Pairwise: level with Egypt (0.22 — Egypt has worse entrapment documentation; Algeria has no equivalent of Egypt's debauchery-law apparatus), above Tunisia (0.19 — active 84-person arrest wave) and Cameroon (0.21 — documented 5-year sentences for trans clothing).
DZA.outOfScopeNotes: Indecency-law application to trans people is documented in aggregate, not per-case; tourism volume is very low.

TUN.name: Tunisia
TUN.summary:
Tunisia is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — the country is in an active crackdown. Between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025, authorities arrested at least 84 people in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity — mostly gay men and transgender women, per Amnesty International. Penal Code Articles 226 bis (public indecency) and 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women.

In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where local NGO Intersection documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as “mental illness.” Since President Saied's 2021 power consolidation, the post-revolution space for LGBT organising (Shams, Damj) has been crushed — Shams was dissolved.

Pairwise: below Egypt (0.22) and Algeria (0.22) on the strength of the current documented arrest wave explicitly including trans women; above Uganda (0.17 — death-penalty statute and lynching culture Tunisia lacks). Tunisia's trajectory is among the world's worst right now.
TUN.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is statutory context; the 2024-25 wave explicitly targeted trans women on gender-identity grounds.

CMR.name: Cameroon
CMR.summary:
Cameroon is High Risk for trans visitors. The Shakiro case is the defining documentation: in February 2021, trans women Shakiro and Patricia were arrested in a Douala restaurant for the clothes they were wearing, convicted of “attempted homosexuality,” “indecent dressing” and ID irregularities, and sentenced to five years. They described five months of “hell” in Douala's central prison, initially in leg chains, before release pending appeal; Shakiro later received asylum in Belgium. Article 347-1 criminalises same-sex acts (up to 5 years), and Cameroon has among Africa's highest prosecution rates.

Police and mob violence against perceived LGBT people are both documented, and there is no legal gender recognition or protection of any kind. The Shakiro conviction shows that visible trans expression in a public place is itself treated as a prosecutable offence.

Pairwise: above Nigeria (0.19 — adds SSMPA mob-lynching culture at scale) and below Egypt (0.22); level with Cameroon-region peers. For a visitor: visible trans presentation in public risks arrest on indecency/ID grounds; prison conditions are severe.
CMR.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; the Shakiro case demonstrates direct application to gender expression.

TZA.name: Tanzania
TZA.summary:
Tanzania is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex activity with up to life imprisonment, and the political environment has been actively hostile since the Magufuli-era crackdowns (arrests, forced anal examinations documented by HRW in earlier years, de-registration of LGBT-serving organisations). The 2024 case of Mauzinde is emblematic: a transgender woman and activist found abandoned in a forest in Rahaleo, beaten, her ears cut off — an attack the UN Human Rights Office called “horrendous.”

OONI documented extensive targeted blocking of LGBTQ websites correlating with the escalating crackdown, and Amnesty's 2024 regional report notes Tanzanian pushes to further criminalise LGBT people. Zanzibar has its own, harsher penal code. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure.

Pairwise: below Tunisia (0.19 — active arrest wave but no life-imprisonment statute) and above Uganda (0.17 — death-penalty statute, though Tanzania's mutilation attack and life-imprisonment law put it in the same tier). For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest under indecency provisions and mob violence; Zanzibar is worse than the mainland.
TZA.outOfScopeNotes: Life-imprisonment statute is same-sex (climate/situational); the Mauzinde attack is trans-specific.

ETH.name: Ethiopia
ETH.summary:
Ethiopia is High Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is criminalised (up to 1 year, or more under aggravating provisions), and because Ethiopia has no legal gender recognition, trans people are legally treated as their birth sex — meaning a trans person's ordinary relationships can be prosecuted as same-sex conduct. The 2024 UPR stakeholder report documents discrimination, violence, and absence of police protection, with trans women and queer women particularly at risk, plus a growing organised anti-LGBTQ+ campaign inside the country.

Documented trans-specific enforcement is thinner than Cameroon's or Tunisia's — Ethiopia's LGBTQ+ community (self-identified as “zega”) is deeply underground, and reporting is sparse — but the legal structure (criminalisation + no LGR catch-all), hostile campaigning, and absence of any protection place it firmly in High Risk. Digital surveillance and blackmail vulnerability are noted in the UPR reporting.

Pairwise: level with Ghana (0.24 — Ghana's near-passed bill signals worse trajectory; Ethiopia's steady-state is worse today), above Tanzania (0.18) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts, visible community, and a 2023 Supreme Court NGO-registration win).
ETH.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation captures trans people via birth-sex legal status — a direct, not situational, mechanism.

LBN.name: Lebanon
LBN.summary:
Lebanon is High Risk for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced, and Cairo 52 documents rising prejudice and violence against trans people, particularly trans women, who face entrenched marginalisation and family/community violence.

Pairwise: above Sri Lanka (0.33 — Lebanon's scene and partial judicial recognition edge it despite the Art 521 statute) and below Kenya (0.38). For a visitor: Beirut is navigable with discretion; visible trans feminine expression carries real (statutory) arrest risk; the economic collapse has degraded police predictability in both directions.
LBN.outOfScopeNotes: LGR case law and healthcare pathologisation are resident-facing; Art 521/534 are the traveler-relevant statutes.

JOR.name: Jordan
JOR.summary:
Jordan is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — the safest of the Levantine Arab states by a clear margin, but on a deteriorating trajectory. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 1951, and courts have granted legal gender recognition in individual cases (the 2014 Court of Cassation ruling — though justified by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex). There is no statute criminalising gender expression itself.

The deterioration is documented: Cairo 52 reports a notable rise in targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, using Ottoman/British-era morality laws; Jordanian security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activities; the 2023 cybercrime law (“inciting immorality”) gives authorities a digital tool against LGBT expression; and gender-affirming surgery is criminalised for trans people (Article 8, Medical and Health Liability Law) while permitted for intersex people. In 2021 security forces arrested 14 people at a private party.

Pairwise: below Turkey (0.47 — comparable legal ambiguity but Turkey's scene and judicial recourse are stronger) and above Kenya (0.38) and Lebanon (0.36 — explicit Art 521 statute). For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression per se, but morality-law discretion, shuttered community infrastructure, and family-society hostility make outing dangerous.
JOR.outOfScopeNotes: Surgery criminalisation and LGR case law are resident-facing; morality-law and cybercrime enforcement are the traveler-relevant mechanisms.

IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.summary:
Iraq is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — it now has one of the world's most explicitly anti-trans statutes, in force since 1 July 2024. Amendments to the 1988 anti-prostitution law criminalise same-sex relationships (10–15 years), “biological sex change based on personal desire and inclination” (criminalising transition itself), and men who “intentionally act like women” (1–3 years) — a direct statutory criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Promoting homosexuality carries a minimum 7-year sentence. President Rashid signed the law on 29 June 2024.

Behind the statute stands a documented milieu of lethal violence: militia-led campaigns against men perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming (HRW's “They Want Us Exterminated” documented mutilated bodies dumped as warnings), with impunity. Most LGBT Iraqis hide their identity entirely. The Kurdistan Region has not passed the federal law but shares the social climate and has no protections.

Pairwise: below Oman (0.09 — similar explicit statute but no militia murder campaigns) and Iran (0.09), above Brunei (0.07) and Saudi Arabia (0.05). For a visitor: being visibly trans is a statutory offence; discovery risks 1–3 years, with severe custodial and militia risk beyond the legal penalty.
IRQ.outOfScopeNotes: The 1988-law amendments apply in federal Iraq; the suspended KRI parliament has not adopted them, but no protection exists there either.

VEN.name: Venezuela
VEN.summary:
Venezuela is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing about gender expression is criminalised, but Venezuela has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid the broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents.

Caracas has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.

Pairwise: above Trinidad & Tobago (0.42 — court-decriminalised with dating-app ambush pattern) and below Peru (0.48 — LGR exists). Venezuela's distinguishing factor is the absence of any legal floor whatsoever plus active regime persecution.
VEN.outOfScopeNotes: General humanitarian and repression context affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific protection vacuum.

BOL.name: Bolivia
BOL.summary:
Bolivia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — one of Latin America's legal pioneers on paper. The 2016 Gender Identity Law was ground-breaking: legal gender recognition on the basis of self-declared identity (administrative process, no surgery), and gender identity is an explicitly protected ground in anti-discrimination law. Bolivia's constitution also names gender identity.

Implementation lags the statute: the first national LGBTQ+ survey (2024) reveals significant exclusion in health, education, employment, and housing; social conservatism is strong outside La Paz/Santa Cruz; and bureaucrats often resist applying the Gender Identity Law. There is no documented pattern of police targeting of trans people as such, and no traveler-facing restriction — but also limited effective protection outside major cities.

Pairwise: below Uruguay (0.81 — comprehensive law plus social acceptance) and Argentina (0.73), above Ecuador (0.57 — now better LGR mechanics but far worse current violence) and Cambodia (0.61). Bolivia's score reflects strong law, weak-but-improving implementation, and moderate social hostility.
BOL.outOfScopeNotes: LGR mechanics and discrimination-law enforcement gaps are resident-facing.

PRY.name: Paraguay
PRY.summary:
Paraguay is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — South America's most conservative country. There is no legal gender recognition (ten lawsuits on trans name recognition remain pending, unresolved), no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. AP documents that many LGBTQ+ Paraguayans feel compelled to leave their hometowns due to discrimination, harassment, and gender-based violence; trans women face particular social rejection. Amnesty reports persistent structural discrimination and high gender-based violence.

Nothing criminalises being trans, Asunción has a small organised community, and there is no documented police targeting pattern — the risk is social hostility and a total protection vacuum rather than state persecution. Tourist traffic is low and there are no documented trans-visitor incidents.

Pairwise: level with the United States (0.50 — very different profiles: Paraguay has no institutional hostility machinery but also no protections anywhere) and China (0.53), below Ecuador (0.57) and Brazil (0.55).
PRY.outOfScopeNotes: Pending LGR lawsuits and discrimination-law absence are resident-facing.

GTM.name: Guatemala
GTM.summary:
Guatemala is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022, with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” law, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (Lambda, trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

Pairwise: level with Honduras (0.39) and below Trinidad & Tobago (0.42). Guatemala's distinguishing factor is the documented murder count plus explicit official exclusion of trans women from protective law.
GTM.outOfScopeNotes: General gang violence affects all travelers; femicide-law exclusion is resident-facing but signals institutional stance.

HND.name: Honduras
HND.summary:
Honduras is High Risk for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

Pairwise: below Guatemala (0.40 — comparable violence; Guatemala's murder counts are higher in absolute terms but Honduras's per-capita pattern and the state-responsibility finding are at least as severe) and above Jamaica (0.31). For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the hemisphere outside Brazil/Mexico.
HND.outOfScopeNotes: Gang violence affects everyone; the score reflects the trans-specific documented pattern and state-responsibility finding.

SLV.name: El Salvador
SLV.summary:
El Salvador is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception with mass arbitrary detention (75,000+ imprisoned, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

Pairwise: above Guatemala (0.40 — the homicide collapse is real and large) and Honduras (0.39), below Trinidad & Tobago (0.42). El Salvador's profile is unique: street-violence probability way down, arbitrary-state-power probability way up.
SLV.outOfScopeNotes: The state of exception affects all travelers; its trans-specific application is a risk mechanism, not a documented pattern.

CRI.name: Costa Rica
CRI.summary:
Costa Rica is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.

Pairwise: level with Poland and Croatia (0.72 — very different profiles; Costa Rica's judicial trajectory is better, its social conservatism comparable), below Chile (0.74 — fuller LGR) and well above Panama (0.63) and the Dominican Republic (0.50).
CRI.outOfScopeNotes: ID sex-marker limits and Church influence are resident-facing/climate.

PAN.name: Panama
PAN.summary:
Panama is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery — a resident-facing barrier. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and in March 2023 the Supreme Court ruled same-sex marriage is not a constitutional right, signaling judicial conservatism. Panama City has a visible, established trans community and hosts regional LGBT organising.

No traveler-facing restrictions exist: no bathroom laws, no border friction, no documented police targeting pattern. Social hostility is moderate — machista culture persists, and trans women face documented employment exclusion — but violent targeting is far below Northern Triangle levels.

Pairwise: level with Bolivia (0.63 — different profiles: Bolivia has self-declaration LGR, Panama has lower social hostility and better infrastructure) and Vietnam (0.63), below Costa Rica (0.72 — the regional outlier), above Cambodia (0.61).
PAN.outOfScopeNotes: Surgery requirement for LGR and marriage ruling are resident-facing.

DOM.name: Dominican Republic
DOM.summary:
The Dominican Republic is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, but strikingly, Articles 210/260 still criminalise it for police and armed-forces members — challenged at the Constitutional Court in August 2024, revealing the institutional culture. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering SOGI (Brazil formally recommended one at the 2024 UPR), and documented violence against trans women is high, particularly affecting the most marginalised.

Tourist zones (Punta Cana, Puerto Plata) are heavily insulated resort enclaves with international norms; Santo Domingo has a visible community and annual Pride caravan. Outside those bubbles, machista culture, police harassment of trans women (especially sex workers), and anti-Haitian dynamics that compound for dark-skinned trans people are documented.

Pairwise: level with the United States and Mexico (0.50 — different profiles: the DR has no institutional hostility machinery like US bathroom laws but a far weaker protection floor), above Trinidad & Tobago (0.42) and below Paraguay (0.52).
DOM.outOfScopeNotes: The police/military sodomy articles do not apply to civilians or visitors; resort vs. non-resort risk differs sharply.

CAN.name: Canada
CAN.summary:
Canada is Low Risk for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveler warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

Pairwise: above Australia (0.85 — comparable, but Canada's federal X marker and earlier statutory protection edge it), below Ireland (0.87) and Denmark (0.87). For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets.
CAN.outOfScopeNotes: Provincial healthcare/school policy rollbacks are resident-facing climate signals.

AUS.name: Australia
AUS.summary:
Australia is Low Risk for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court's landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024; self-declaration birth-certificate reform has spread to most jurisdictions. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse. State-level LGR remains a patchwork (not all jurisdictions are self-ID).

Pairwise: below Canada (0.86 — federal X marker, earlier uniform protection) and above New Zealand (0.84 — NZ's 42% hate-crime jump and police-failure documentation outweigh Australia's current climate). For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability.
AUS.outOfScopeNotes: State LGR patchwork and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing.

NZL.name: New Zealand
NZL.summary:
New Zealand is Low Risk for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration has been in force since 2023 (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act); the Law Commission reviewed Human Rights Act protections for trans, non-binary and intersex people in 2024; and takatāpui/rainbow communities have deep institutional recognition. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

The counterweights are documented and significant: reports of gender-identity hate crimes jumped 42% between 2022 and 2023 (161 to 229 incidents), spiking around the Posie Parker visit; the Counting Ourselves survey found almost 1 in 5 trans and non-binary people were threatened with physical violence in four years, and 8% experienced it; and community advocates accuse police of failing rainbow communities amid far-right agitation (library events crashed, church arson threats). New Zealand's global-progressive reputation outruns its current street climate.

Pairwise: below Australia (0.85 — comparable law, but NZ's documented 2023 hate-crime spike and police-failure pattern are worse) and above Germany (0.83). For a visitor: full legal protection; moderate probability of harassment in charged spaces; functioning (if criticised) institutions.
NZL.outOfScopeNotes: Counting Ourselves data is resident-survey-based; healthcare gaps are resident-facing.

ALB.name: Albania
ALB.summary:
Albania is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; a National LGBTI Action Plan (2021–2027) is in force (implementation is admittedly flawed); and the UN Independent Expert on SOGI conducted a full country visit in July 2024 — a sign of government openness unusual for the region. Tirana hosts an annual Pride. There is no legal gender recognition (Albania rejected a self-ID recommendation at its UPR), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and discrimination in key areas drew European Parliament concern.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, no bathroom laws, no documented police targeting; the realistic risk is social hostility outside Tirana and along more conservative rural areas. EU candidate status is driving slow alignment.

Pairwise: level with Serbia (0.64 — comparable climate; Albania's action plan vs Serbia's larger community infrastructure) and below Moldova (0.65 — SOGI hate-crime law) and Montenegro (0.66 — partnership law).
ALB.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and action-plan implementation gaps are resident-facing.

MKD.name: North Macedonia
MKD.summary:
North Macedonia is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised, and Skopje hosts both Pride and an organised Trans March for Visibility (TransFormA, March 2024) — public trans organising that proceeds without serious incident. Anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and gender identity (2019 amendments). Counterweights: hate speech and hate crimes remain common with no effective justice-system response (European Commission), social-media death threats are routine, and there is no legal gender recognition.

Pairwise: below Albania (0.64) and Serbia (0.64) — the documented justice-system non-response to hate crime edges it down — and above Bosnia (0.61) and Ukraine (0.62). For a visitor: no legal exposure; small but functioning community; standard Balkan street-hostility caution.
MKD.outOfScopeNotes: Justice-system non-response and LGR absence are resident-facing/climate.

MNE.name: Montenegro
MNE.summary:
Montenegro is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — the Western Balkans' most advanced legal framework. It has a same-sex partnership law (2020), anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and SOGI-inclusive hate-crime provisions; Podgorica Pride proceeds annually. Counterweights documented by ILGA-Europe: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric is a serious issue, and misdemeanour charges are overused in place of proper hate-crime prosecution (European Commission). There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative practice is inconsistent).

Pairwise: above Moldova (0.65), level with Romania (0.67), and — after the 2026-08 audit — above Hungary (0.68)? No: the audit found Montenegro’s framework (partnership law + SOGI hate-crime provisions + protected Pride) objectively stronger than Hungary’s (propaganda law in force + LGR ban + German court’s extradition-refusal finding). MNE raised to 0.67, effectively tied with ROU and above HUN 0.68 is superseded: HUN sits at 0.68 by its own anchors; MNE at 0.67 reflects slightly thinner implementation. For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, small tolerant coastal tourist scene; standard caution in the north.
MNE.outOfScopeNotes: LGR inconsistency and prosecution-practice gaps are resident-facing.

BIH.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
BIH.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; Sarajevo Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 with heavy (necessary) police protection; and most cantons have now appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes — genuine institutional progress. Counterweights from the 2024 Pink Report: negative events are accumulating, the trend is unfavourable outside Sarajevo (especially Republika Srpska), and trans people occupy a “precarious position” — no legal gender recognition framework, restricted healthcare access, and institutional suspicion. The state is also deeply dysfunctional generally.

Pairwise: below North Macedonia (0.62 — MKD's anti-discrimination law is stronger) and above Cambodia (0.61, tie — different profiles). For a visitor: no legal exposure; stick to Sarajevo and tourist areas; avoid visible trans presentation in Republika Srpska and rural areas.
BIH.outOfScopeNotes: Entity-level (Republika Srpska) hostility varies; LGR absence is resident-facing.

GEO.name: Georgia
GEO.summary:
Georgia is High Risk for trans visitors — and deteriorating fast. In September 2024 parliament passed the Russia-style law “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”: it bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, LGBT public assembly, and dissemination of LGBT information — the region's harshest legislative package outside Russia itself. One day after passage, Kesaria Abramidze, one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her Tbilisi apartment; mourners and AP drew a direct line between the law's rhetoric and the killing.

This compounds an existing pattern: the 2021 Pride office ransacking by far-right mobs while police stood by, the foreign-agents law choking LGBT NGOs (which refuse to register and face bankruptcy), and documented police failure to protect demonstrators (Identoba v. Georgia ECtHR line of cases, still unimplemented). Georgia's visible trans community is now legally erased and physically targeted.

Pairwise: below Turkey (0.47 — no such legislative package) and Armenia (0.46), level with Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation climate; Georgia's new statutory package is arguably worse, Kenya's mob culture is worse; net tie). For a visitor: being visibly trans in Georgia now carries both statutory risk (assembly/information provisions) and elevated street-violence risk, with police as unreliable protectors.
GEO.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 law’s healthcare and LGR provisions are resident-facing; its assembly/information provisions can reach visitors.

ARM.name: Armenia
ARM.summary:
Armenia is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Armenia has no anti-LGBT legislation of the Georgian or Russian type — and an administrative practice for legal gender recognition exists (medicalised). Pink Armenia's 2024 annual report documents ongoing violations including inhuman/degrading treatment, and hate speech is routine in public discourse; the 2018 failed anti-discrimination bill means there is still no SOGI-specific protection statute. Yerevan has a small organised community (Pink Armenia, Right Side — a trans-led NGO), but visibility carries real risk.

Pairwise: below Turkey (0.47 — comparable; Turkey has more institutional infrastructure, Armenia less state-led hostility) and above Georgia (0.38 — Armenia has no equivalent legislative package and no recent trans murder). For a visitor: no legal exposure; social hostility significant outside central Yerevan; police response unreliable.
ARM.outOfScopeNotes: Protection-statute absence and LGR medicalisation are resident-facing.

AZE.name: Azerbaijan
AZE.summary:
Azerbaijan is High Risk for trans visitors. The documented pattern is grim: a trans woman was tortured and murdered in Baku in July 2023; a second trans woman's murder in March 2024 was met with a police response lacking comprehensive investigation; several other trans people were physically assaulted, including by police themselves; and two trans women were detained for “hooliganism” for making noise. Government-affiliated media air targeted discriminatory hate speech. Trans people face total economic marginalisation (black-market work, precarious housing).

Nothing formally criminalises gender expression, but police are perpetrators rather than protectors, and the state is one of the world's more closed authoritarian systems — there is no recourse and no community infrastructure that can operate openly. An April 2024 ECtHR ruling found violations in Azerbaijan's treatment of LGBTI applicants.

Pairwise: below Sri Lanka (0.33 — comparable police-perpetrator pattern, but Sri Lanka has functioning NGOs and court recourse) and above Malaysia (0.28). For a visitor: no statute bars entry or expression, but discovery risks police abuse with no remedy, and the murder-impunity pattern is documented.
AZE.outOfScopeNotes: Economic exclusion data is resident-facing; police-perpetrator pattern is traveler-relevant.

KAZ.name: Kazakhstan
KAZ.summary:
Kazakhstan is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — Central Asia's most liveable country for trans people, which is a relative statement. Nothing is criminalised; legal gender recognition exists (heavily medicalised: psychiatric boards, and surgery requirements applied in practice); and revealingly, hundreds of trans people fled TO Kazakhstan from Russia after its propaganda law and LGR ban. ODIHR recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in 2024 — real, but documented and reported, which itself indicates functioning civil society (Feminita, ECOM).

The trajectory is the concern: a “We Are Against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda” petition gained official review by the Ministry of Culture in 2024 (HRW urged rejection), and anti-gender MPs are vocal. Currently there is no propaganda statute, no bathroom law, and no police targeting pattern — police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

Pairwise: level with Peru (0.48) and just below the USA/Mexico (0.50) — Kazakhstan has no institutional hostility machinery but a far weaker protection floor — and above Armenia (0.46) and Turkey (0.47). For a visitor: no legal exposure; low visibility = low risk; Almaty/Astana are navigable.
KAZ.outOfScopeNotes: LGR medicalisation and the propaganda petition are resident-facing/trajectory signals.

UZB.name: Uzbekistan
UZB.summary:
Uzbekistan is High Risk for trans visitors. Article 120 of the Criminal Code criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 3 years) — and Human Dignity Trust notes transgender people may be targeted under it, since there is no legal gender recognition and trans people are legally their birth sex. There is substantial evidence of recent enforcement: frequent arrests, and extortion by threat of arrest, with police as the most common perpetrators of anti-LGBT violence; torture goes unpunished (HRW). Because of criminalisation, victims cannot report violence to authorities.

ECOM's 2024 national report documents continuing rights violations, and the Justice Ministry denies registration to independent human-rights groups — no community infrastructure can operate openly. There is no documented trans-visitor case, but the legal mechanism (birth-sex status + Art 120) means a trans visitor discovered in a same-sex-appearing relationship faces direct prosecution risk, and discovery itself invites extortion.

Pairwise: level with Egypt (0.22 — Egypt's entrapment machinery is more systematic; Uzbekistan's extortion pattern is comparable) and Algeria (0.22), below Morocco (0.25) and above Tunisia (0.19).
UZB.outOfScopeNotes: Art 120 formally applies to male same-sex conduct; its application to trans people is via birth-sex legal status — a direct mechanism, not merely climate.
