NIC.name: Nicaragua
NIC.summary:
Nicaragua is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans (sodomy was decriminalised in 2008), but NGOs document 108 cases of violence against the LGTBIQ+ community in 2024 alone, and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years. Since 2018 the Ortega regime has shut down or exiled virtually all independent civil society — including LGBT organisations — so there is no domestic protection infrastructure and no recourse; arbitrary detention is used broadly against perceived opponents.

Pairwise: level with El Salvador (0.41 — different profiles: NIC has state-suppression of all NGOs plus trans murders; SLV has gang-violence collapse plus arbitrary-detention state), above Guatemala (0.40) and below Trinidad & Tobago (0.42).
NIC.outOfScopeNotes: Generalised repression affects all; the trans-murder count is trans-specific.

GUY.name: Guyana
GUY.summary:
Guyana is High Risk for trans visitors — one of only five Western-Hemisphere countries still criminalising same-sex conduct (buggery carries life imprisonment on paper, though rarely enforced). The IACHR heard evidence in November 2024 of severe violence against trans women: 69 cases of violence against trans women documented 2018–2022, in a country of under a million people. Police fail to investigate anti-LGBT violence; there is no anti-discrimination legislation (the UN Human Rights Committee called for it in April 2024) and no legal gender recognition.

Cross-dressing was decriminalised after a 2018 CCJ ruling (McEwan v AG), removing the most direct trans-expression statute, but the climate and investigative failure keep risk high. Georgetown has a small organised community (SASOD).

Pairwise: level with Sri Lanka (0.33 — both criminalisation-plus-police-failure profiles), above Jamaica (0.31 — Jamaica's mob-killing culture is worse), below Lebanon (0.36).
GUY.outOfScopeNotes: Buggery statutes are rarely enforced (climate/situational); the CCJ struck cross-dressing laws in 2018.

SUR.name: Suriname
SUR.summary:
Suriname is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — legally unremarkable, socially mixed. Same-sex conduct is legal; the constitution's “any other status” clause is read to cover SOGI discrimination; and the 2022 Equal Treatment Labour Act added employment protections. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-murder pattern, but Paramaribo's small community reports routine harassment, and the interior has essentially no protection.

Pairwise: above Ecuador (0.57 — far less violence) and below India (0.58, tie). For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest street risk in Paramaribo; low tourist infrastructure generally.
SUR.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and interior governance gaps are resident-facing.

KGZ.name: Kyrgyzstan
KGZ.summary:
Kyrgyzstan is High Risk for trans visitors — once Central Asia's relative haven, now regressing. In 2023-2024 Kyrgyzstan adopted two discriminatory laws targeting the LGBTI community and restricting LGBTI organisations, accompanied by homophobic/transphobic MP rhetoric; TGEU records Kyrgyzstan (2021) among the countries that removed legal gender recognition entirely (the 2020 Civil Status Acts law blocks birth-certificate changes). Same-sex conduct is legal (1998), but police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and the community (Kyrgyz Indigo) operates under pressure.

Pairwise: level with Lebanon (0.36 — different mechanisms: KGZ has NGO-restriction laws and LGR removal; LBN has Art 521/534), below Georgia (0.38 — Georgia's 2024 package is broader) and above Sri Lanka (0.33). For a visitor: no expression statute, but LGR removal + police extortion culture + active anti-LGBT political campaign make outing risky.
KGZ.outOfScopeNotes: LGR removal is resident-facing; NGO-restriction laws signal the enforcement climate.

TJK.name: Tajikistan
TJK.summary:
Tajikistan is High Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation (IPHR 2024) shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition (a medicalised registration route exists on paper under the Civil Status Acts law), no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

Pairwise: level with Malaysia (0.28 — different mechanisms: TJK has police raids without statutes; MYS has Sharia statutes), below Azerbaijan (0.30) and above Pakistan (0.26). For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids + registry practices + zero recourse make discovery dangerous.
TJK.outOfScopeNotes: Registry practices and raid patterns target residents but define the enforcement climate for any discovered trans person.

TKM.name: Turkmenistan
TKM.summary:
Turkmenistan is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 2 years under Article 135) and, more fundamentally, Turkmenistan is one of the world's most closed states: the state exerts strict media control and heavy internet monitoring, no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible since 2019, and asylum is the community's most urgent need (ILGA-Europe). Amnesty has documented systematic abuses. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, no recourse, and no visibility — the only safe strategy is total concealment.

Pairwise: level with Qatar (0.12 — different profiles: TKM's opacity prevents even documenting abuse; QAT's abuse is documented), below Uzbekistan (0.22 — UZB has enforcement data and some civil society) and Russia (0.12, tie). For a visitor: any discoverable online presence or visible nonconformity is dangerous in a state that monitors communications pervasively.
TKM.outOfScopeNotes: Absence of documentation is itself evidence of severity: data collection is impossible because it is unsafe.

SYR.name: Syria
SYR.summary:
Syria is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Articles 520/517 of the Penal Code criminalise “sexual acts against nature” and public indecency; there is no legal gender recognition. Since the fall of the Assad regime (December 2024), the situation has worsened: the Guardians of Equality Movement documented “waves of violence” against Syrian transgender women in the first two months of 2025, implicating both non-state armed groups and security forces in multiple cities, and February 2025 videos showed authorities arresting trans women. Digital targeting (entrapment via apps, extortion) is documented across the conflict period.

Pairwise: above Saudi Arabia (0.05 — SYR's chaos vs SAU's systematic state machinery) and below Iraq (0.08 — IRQ now has a codified anti-trans statute; SYR has codified indecency + active violence waves). For a visitor: active conflict, trans-targeted violence waves, no recourse whatsoever.
SYR.outOfScopeNotes: General conflict risk affects all; the 2025 trans-women violence waves are trans-specific.

LBY.name: Libya
LBY.summary:
Libya is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “illicit sexual intercourse” and “indecent acts” (up to 5 years), and Cairo 52 documents de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and transition through these provisions — compounded by recent religious rulings declaring the very term “gender” haram, making anyone using it in media or institutions susceptible to prosecution. Militias control territory and operate detention sites where torture is systematic; there is no functioning central judiciary, no LGR, and no protection of any kind.

Pairwise: level with Oman (0.09 — OMN has an explicit enforced statute; LBY has de-facto criminalisation plus militia detention risk), below Iraq (0.08, comparable) and above Syria (0.06). For a visitor: detention by any of several militia authorities is the modal bad outcome, with no consular reach in much of the country.
LBY.outOfScopeNotes: Militia fragmentation means enforcement varies by territory; the trans-specific mechanism is documented de-facto criminalisation.

YEM.name: Yemen
YEM.summary:
Yemen is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The legal framework criminalises same-sex conduct (up to death under some interpretations of the Penal Code; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise), but Cairo 52 emphasises the operative mechanism: the erosion of the rule of law and the power of militias has facilitated a surge in attacks targeting transgender individuals — de facto criminalisation operating outside any judicial system. Houthi-controlled areas impose their own moral-policing regime; the south has its own militia authorities.

Pairwise: level with Syria (0.06 — both are active-conflict states where trans people are targeted extra-judicially), above Afghanistan (0.02 — AFG's Taliban system is more totalising and systematic) and below Iraq (0.08). For a visitor: no safe authority to appeal to anywhere in the country.
YEM.outOfScopeNotes: War risk affects all; the documented surge in trans-targeted attacks is trans-specific.

BTN.name: Bhutan
BTN.summary:
Bhutan is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally (Pride Bhutan, Rainbow Bhutan). The government engages with UNFPA's Free & Equal campaign at the level of the Royal Court of Justice and Cabinet. Trans women report violence and discrimination remain widespread (trans people 4x more likely to experience assault), and there is no legal gender recognition, but there is no criminalisation, no police targeting pattern, and a monarchy-led culture that discourages open aggression.

Pairwise: above Nepal (0.64 — Nepal has stronger jurisprudence but Bhutan lower reported violence) and below Romania (0.67). Tourism is tightly regulated (daily fee system), which incidentally provides visitors a structured, monitored environment.

LAO.name: Laos
LAO.summary:
Laos is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, and Laos has a socially visible tradition of trans feminine people; but there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, no registered LGBT organisation (the one-party state restricts all civil society), and no documented recourse. Vientiane and Luang Prabang are accustomed to tourists; the risk is administrative (an opaque state) more than violent.

Pairwise: below Cambodia (0.61 — functioning NGOs, UPR engagement) and Vietnam (0.63), above China (0.53) and Myanmar (0.15).
LAO.outOfScopeNotes: Civil-society restrictions affect all; no trans-specific mechanism documented.

TLS.name: Timor-Leste
TLS.summary:
Timor-Leste is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's equality provisions have been read inclusively, and Dili hosts an annual Pride march with government participation — remarkable for a young, Catholic-majority nation. There is no legal gender recognition and services are thin, but there is no documented pattern of police targeting or anti-trans violence, and the small community (CODIVA, Arco Iris) operates openly.

Pairwise: level with Panama (0.63) and Bolivia (0.63), above Cambodia (0.61) and below Moldova (0.65). For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest infrastructure; low documented hostility.
TLS.outOfScopeNotes: Service thinness and LGR absence are resident-facing.

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea
PNG.summary:
Papua New Guinea is High Risk for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years), and PNG has extreme levels of gender-based violence generally — among the world's highest documented rates. Port Moresby and Lae are dangerous cities for everyone; tribal-justice dynamics and police brutality affect marginalised people severely. There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and sorcery-accusation violence shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

Pairwise: level with Cameroon (0.21 — both pair criminalisation with extreme ambient violence), above Nigeria (0.19) and below Egypt (0.22). For a visitor: the trans-specific risk is inseparable from the general security situation, which is among the worst in the Pacific.
PNG.outOfScopeNotes: General security conditions affect all travelers severely; criminalisation is the trans-relevant mechanism.

BWA.name: Botswana
BWA.summary:
Botswana is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — Africa's strongest judicial record after South Africa. The High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2019 (Letsweletse Motshidiemang v AG, upheld 2021); the Court of Appeal ordered the government to register LEGABIBO; and trans people have won document-change cases (ND v Attorney General, 2017). Draft 2024 constitutional changes even contemplate intersex rights. Implementation lags the rulings (SALC documents unsatisfactory compliance), social conservatism persists, and there is no general LGR statute — but the courts are a genuine protection, unique in the region.

Pairwise: just below South Africa (0.66 — SA has constitutional protection and fuller infrastructure; BWA's recent jurisprudence is comparable but its implementation record is weaker) and above Serbia (0.64). For a visitor: decriminalised, functioning courts, moderate social hostility.
BWA.outOfScopeNotes: LGR requires litigation per-case; implementation gaps are resident-facing.

NAM.name: Namibia
NAM.summary:
Namibia is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Courts have delivered important rulings (the 2023 Digashu recognition of foreign same-sex marriages; earlier document-change wins for trans people), but same-sex conduct between men technically remains criminalised under the common law (the 2024 High Court declined to strike it, and parliament passed hostile marriage bills), and implementation of pro-LGBT rulings is documented as unsatisfactory (SALC). Windhoek has a small organised community (Equal Namibia); police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

Pairwise: below Botswana (0.65 — BWA decriminalised; NAM retains the common-law crime and legislative backlash) and above Brazil (0.55, tie). For a visitor: enforcement of the old law is essentially nil, but the legal floor is hostile and the politics are deteriorating.
NAM.outOfScopeNotes: Common-law criminalisation is unenforced but real; implementation gaps are resident-facing.

MUS.name: Mauritius
MUS.summary:
Mauritius is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — the Indian Ocean's most liveable jurisdiction. The Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct; the Equal Opportunities Act covers discrimination; and in 2024 Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan competed as the first trans woman in Miss Universe Mauritius — a public milestone met with national discussion rather than violence. There is no legal gender recognition law (a barrier highlighted by AfricLaw), and social conservatism persists, but tourist infrastructure is extensive and accustomed to diverse visitors, and there is no documented police targeting pattern.

Pairwise: below Seychelles-region comparators and level with Latvia (0.69)/Israel (0.69) — above Hungary (0.68). For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning courts, low street risk in tourist areas.
MUS.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and recognition gaps are resident-facing.

SYC.name: Seychelles
SYC.summary:
Seychelles is Reduced Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016; the constitution guarantees equal protection; and the country is a small, tourism-dependent archipelago with extremely low violent crime and long exposure to international visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-specific infrastructure, but also no documented pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.

Pairwise: level with Poland/Croatia/Costa Rica (0.72 — different profiles; Seychelles lacks their legal infrastructure but has lower hostility), above Mauritius (0.70 — MUS has the Equal Opportunities Act and 2023 decriminalisation ruling; SYC edges it on ambient safety) and below Chile (0.74).
SYC.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence is resident-facing; evidence is thin given the tiny population.

SEN.name: Senegal
SEN.summary:
Senegal is High Risk for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “unnatural acts” (up to 5 years, applied to both men and women), enforcement is active (periodic arrest waves), and anti-LGBT forces are pushing to raise sentences to 15 years. Mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented, and even public discussion is policed: two men were jailed in 2024 for “false news” after accusing the Prime Minister of tolerating homosexuality. There is no legal gender recognition and no visible community infrastructure — Dakar's scene is deeply underground.

Pairwise: below Malaysia (0.28 — comparable criminalisation-plus-mob climate) and above Pakistan (0.26) and Côte d'Ivoire (0.34 — CIV decriminalised but has the 2024 hunt-down violence wave; SEN has statutory criminalisation but no equivalent mob-hunt wave; net SEN slightly worse). For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest and mob violence.
SEN.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; mob violence is documented climate.

CIV.name: Côte d'Ivoire
CIV.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is High Risk for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Long considered West Africa's tolerant outlier (same-sex conduct has never been criminalised), the country saw a wave of violence in late 2024: social-media influencers exhorted followers to “hunt” gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed (NYT, Oct 2024). There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection; police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

Pairwise: above Senegal (0.27 — SEN has criminalisation; CIV does not but has the active hunt wave) and below Kenya (0.38 — KEN criminalises but has stronger courts and civil society). For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in Abidjan.
CIV.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 violence wave targeted perceived gay men primarily but gender-nonconforming people are the most visible targets.

MLI.name: Mali
MLI.summary:
Mali is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

Pairwise: level with Nigeria (0.19)/Cameroon (0.21) — below Tunisia (0.19, comparable) and above Uganda (0.17). For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.
MLI.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 penal code application to trans expression is via indecency provisions; drafting vagueness noted by HDT.

BFA.name: Burkina Faso
BFA.summary:
Burkina Faso is High Risk for trans visitors. In July 2024 the military junta approved a revised Personal and Family Code criminalising homosexuality — Burkina Faso had never previously outlawed it. The junta (Traoré) has clamped down on opposition and media, promised elections have not been held, and much of the country faces jihadist insurgency. Enforcement details of the new law remain unclear (HDT notes drafting uncertainty), but the direction and the absence of any institutional recourse are unambiguous.

Pairwise: level with Egypt/Algeria/Uzbekistan (0.22), above Mali (0.20 — MLI's code is harsher and more explicitly enforced) and below Ghana (0.24). For a visitor: new criminalisation under a junta, plus severe general security conditions.
BFA.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 family-code criminalisation is new; enforcement practice not yet documented.

MOZ.name: Mozambique
MOZ.summary:
Mozambique is Elevated Risk for trans visitors — one of Africa's better legal positions. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 Penal Code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register (Lambda Mozambique); and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. Counterweights: no legal gender recognition, no SOGI hate-crime statute, social hostility outside Maputo is significant, and the Cabo Delgado insurgency affects the north (a general, not trans-specific, risk).

Pairwise: level with Namibia (0.56 — MOZ decriminalised legislatively, NAM has stronger courts but retained common-law crime) and below Ecuador (0.57). For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest infrastructure; avoid the north.
MOZ.outOfScopeNotes: Cabo Delgado insurgency is a general risk; LGR absence is resident-facing.

RWA.name: Rwanda
RWA.summary:
Rwanda is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations). There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and civil society operates within the regime's tight limits.

Pairwise: level with Venezuela (0.44 — different profiles: RWA has lower violence, more arbitrary state power) and above Trinidad & Tobago (0.42). For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil.
RWA.outOfScopeNotes: Sweep detentions are documented against trans persons specifically (2025 HRF submission).

AGO.name: Angola
AGO.summary:
Angola is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.

Pairwise: above Mozambique (0.56 — AGO's statutory package is stronger) and below India (0.58). For a visitor: no legal exposure and formal anti-discrimination law; social hostility moderate-high outside Luanda.
AGO.outOfScopeNotes: Statutory protections vs implementation gap documented by Angolan CSOs.

COD.name: DR Congo
COD.summary:
DR Congo is High Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised — but the reality on the ground is severe insecurity: mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented, police extortion is routine, the east is an active conflict zone (M23), and LGBT organisations (Savie asbl in Bukavu) report systematic violations in their 2024 UPR submission. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure; Kinshasa's small scene is underground.

Pairwise: level with Azerbaijan (0.30 — different profiles: AZE has police-perpetrator pattern in a functional state; COD has state absence and mob dynamics), below Sri Lanka (0.33). For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but outing risks mob violence with no effective state protection anywhere in the country.
COD.outOfScopeNotes: Conflict conditions in the east are general; mob justice against LGBT people is documented in UPR submissions.

ZMB.name: Zambia
ZMB.summary:
Zambia is High Risk for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) with documented recent enforcement: Amnesty International's November 2024 campaign highlights Madalitso Zulu, serving a 15-year sentence with hard labour; Amnesty's 2024 regional report documents rising hostility in Zambia. There is no legal gender recognition, religious leaders lead anti-LGBT mobilisation, and police are perpetrators more than protectors.

Pairwise: level with Ghana (0.24 — both criminalisation-plus-mobilised-hostility), above Zimbabwe (0.27, actually below — ZMB's documented 15-year serving sentence and current campaign edge it below ZWE) and below Morocco (0.25). For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest; the documented serving-sentence case shows courts impose maximum terms.
ZMB.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; trans people are captured via birth-sex status and indecency provisions.

ZWE.name: Zimbabwe
ZWE.summary:
Zimbabwe is High Risk for trans visitors. The 2006 Criminal Law Act criminalises sodomy (up to 1 year — a lighter formal penalty than neighbours, though indecency provisions add exposure), and Amnesty's 2024 report documents shrinking civic space threatening LGBT organising (GALZ operates under pressure; its offices have been raided historically). There is no legal gender recognition, political rhetoric is hostile, and mob violence is documented — but prosecution under the sodomy law is rarer than in Zambia, and a small organised community persists openly enough to litigate.

Pairwise: above Zambia (0.24 — ZWE's formal penalty is lighter and enforcement rarer) and below Senegal (0.27, tie). For a visitor: statutory exposure exists but enforcement is sporadic; social hostility is the main risk.
ZWE.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; enforcement pattern is sporadic.

MWI.name: Malawi
MWI.summary:
Malawi is High Risk for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) AND Human Dignity Trust lists Malawi as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. A moratorium on prosecutions has held since 2014, but in June 2024 the Constitutional Court upheld the ban — a case brought partly by a local trans woman and her Dutch partner — and religious leaders led nationwide anti-LGBT marches in 2023. Discrimination and violence are regular despite the moratorium.

Pairwise: above Zambia (0.24 — ZMB has an active 15-year serving case; MWI's moratorium holds) and below Zimbabwe (0.27, comparable). The gender-expression criminalisation listing is what places MWI in the mid-0.2s rather than higher.
MWI.outOfScopeNotes: Prosecution moratorium is informal and revocable; the 2024 ruling keeps the statute fully alive.

SDN.name: Sudan
SDN.summary:
Sudan is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Article 152 of the Penal Code criminalises gender nonconformity directly; sodomy carries life imprisonment (capital/corporal punishment removed in 2020 reforms); and Cairo 52 documents state violence against LGBTQIA+ people including extrajudicial killings. Since April 2023 the country has been in a catastrophic civil war (SAF vs RSF) with documented mass atrocities — the conflict intensifies every risk and eliminates any recourse. There is no LGR and no community infrastructure.

Pairwise: level with Iraq (0.08 — IRQ has a codified anti-trans statute; SDN has Art 152 + active civil war) and above Syria/Yemen (0.06 — SDN's legal system, though hostile, nominally exists where SAF controls territory). For a visitor: statutory criminalisation of gender nonconformity plus one of the world's worst active conflicts.
SDN.outOfScopeNotes: War conditions affect all; Art 152 is trans-specific.

SSD.name: South Sudan
SSD.summary:
South Sudan is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. The 2008 Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years), and Human Dignity Trust lists South Sudan as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. The country has barely emerged from civil war, state institutions are vestigial outside Juba, communal violence is endemic, and there is no documented LGBT community infrastructure whatsoever — no organisation can operate openly. No trans-specific case is documented because documentation itself is nearly impossible.

Pairwise: above Sudan (0.08 — SSD's formal penalties are lower and its wartime is less acute in 2026) and below Belarus (0.13). For a visitor: statutory risk plus a near-total absence of protective institutions.
SSD.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation absence reflects state incapacity; gender-expression criminalisation is statutory.

SOM.name: Somalia
SOM.summary:
Somalia is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — one of the world's most dangerous countries for any LGBT person. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 3 years), but the operative reality is worse: Al-Shabaab controls significant territory and applies its interpretation of sharia, under which homosexuality and gender transgression are capital offences — executions are documented. Even in government areas, mob violence and clan-justice dynamics make any gender nonconformity lethal-risk. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, and no recourse of any kind.

Pairwise: above Afghanistan (0.02 — AFG's Taliban control is more total and systematic; SOM's is fragmented between a weak government and Al-Shabaab) and below Syria (0.06). For a visitor: there is no safe way to be visibly trans anywhere in Somalia.
SOM.outOfScopeNotes: Fragmented authority means enforcement varies; Al-Shabaab areas apply capital punishment.

ERI.name: Eritrea
ERI.summary:
Eritrea is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Article 310(1) of the 2015 Penal Code criminalises “homosexual conduct” (up to 7 years), there are no anti-discrimination protections of any kind, and Eritrea is among the world's most closed states — indefinite national service, mass arbitrary detention, no independent media, no civil society, and no way to document conditions. Eritrea has rejected every SOGI recommendation at every UPR cycle. Nothing is known about trans people in Eritrea because nothing can be known — the absence of data reflects total informational control.

Pairwise: level with South Sudan (0.10 — different profiles: ERI is a functioning totalitarian state; SSD is a failing one) and below Turkmenistan (0.12, comparable opacity but lower penalties) and above Somalia (0.04).
ERI.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation absence reflects totalitarian informational control.

ATG.name: Antigua and Barbuda
ATG.summary: Antigua and Barbuda is Elevated Risk. The High Court struck down the buggery/gross-indecency laws in July 2022, reading the constitutional bar on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. No LGR, no anti-discrimination statute, and residual social hostility; tourist resort areas are insulated. Pairwise: level with Ecuador (0.57)/Mozambique (0.56) region of the scale, below Suriname (0.58).
ATG.outOfScopeNotes: Decriminalisation is recent; social climate lags the courts.

BRB.name: Barbados
BRB.summary: Barbados is Elevated Risk. Courts struck down the buggery laws in 2022; Barbados has an organised community (Equals, B-GLAD) and a functioning state. No LGR; modest social conservatism; tourist areas accustomed to diverse visitors. Pairwise: level with Suriname (0.58), above Antigua (0.55), below Trinidad & Tobago (0.42)? No — above TTO: Barbados decriminalised via courts with less documented street violence than TTO's Grindr-ambush pattern.

KNA.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
KNA.summary: Saint Kitts and Nevis is Elevated Risk. Part of the Eastern Caribbean decriminalisation wave (2022 court ruling); tiny population, tourist economy, no documented anti-trans violence pattern; no LGR. Pairwise: level with Antigua (0.55).
KNA.outOfScopeNotes: Thin data; inherits Eastern Caribbean profile.

DMA.name: Dominica
DMA.summary: Dominica is Elevated Risk. High Court decriminalised same-sex relations in April 2024 (fourth Eastern Caribbean state); the old law had allowed forced psychiatric commitment. No LGR; small community; no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Pairwise: just below Antigua (0.55 — Dominica's ruling is newer, community thinner).

LCA.name: Saint Lucia
LCA.summary: Saint Lucia is Elevated Risk. The Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down buggery/gross-indecency laws in July 2025 (Randall Theodule v AG) — the region's most recent decriminalisation, welcomed by the IACHR. Saint Lucia has a relatively organised community (ECADE, United and Strong) and hosts Pride. No LGR. Pairwise: level with Barbados (0.58)/Antigua (0.55) cluster, above Dominica (0.54).

VCT.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
VCT.summary: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is Elevated Risk — the Eastern Caribbean outlier: its High Court UPHELD the buggery laws in 2024 (unlike its neighbours), so criminalisation (10 years) remains formally in force. Enforcement is rare, but the legal floor and judicial hostility distinguish it from the decriminalised neighbours. Pairwise: below Dominica (0.54), above Trinidad & Tobago (0.42).
VCT.outOfScopeNotes: 2024 ruling upheld criminalisation — opposite trajectory from neighbours.

GRD.name: Grenada
GRD.summary: Grenada is Elevated Risk. The buggery law (10 years) remains on the books (no successful court challenge yet), though unenforced; no LGR; small community; tourist areas insulated. Pairwise: just below Saint Vincent (0.45), above Trinidad & Tobago (0.42).

BHS.name: Bahamas
BHS.summary: The Bahamas is Elevated Risk. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 1991; tourism-dependent economy with extensive international exposure; no LGR; documented social hostility but no criminalisation and no police-targeting pattern. Pairwise: level with Antigua (0.55), above Jamaica (0.31 — stark contrast: BHS decriminalised decades ago).

BLZ.name: Belize
BLZ.summary: Belize is Elevated Risk. The Court of Appeal struck down the sodomy law in 2016 (Orozco v AG) — the Caribbean's first decriminalisation ruling; Belize has an organised community (UNIBAM) and anti-discrimination employment protection. No LGR; gang violence in Belize City is a general risk. Pairwise: above Barbados (0.58)? — no, level-below at 0.57; above Antigua (0.55).
BLZ.outOfScopeNotes: No LGR; Belize City violence is general.

HTI.name: Haiti
HTI.summary: Haiti is High Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the state has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of Port-au-Prince, the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no LGR, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary. The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled territory can be lethal. Pairwise: level with Azerbaijan/DR Congo (0.30), below Lebanon (0.36).
HTI.outOfScopeNotes: State collapse is general; mob violence against LGBT people documented.

FJI.name: Fiji
FJI.summary: Fiji is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — the Pacific islands' leader. Same-sex relations decriminalised in 2010; the 2013 Constitution bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity AND expression — reportedly the only constitution in the world with that explicit pairing. Counterweights: no gender-marker change mechanism, and the Asia Pacific Transgender Network documents high rates of violence and harassment against trans people. Suva has an organised community (Haus of Khameleon, Rainbow Pride Foundation). Pairwise: level with Panama/Bolivia/Timor-Leste (0.63), below Nepal (0.64).
FJI.outOfScopeNotes: Constitutional protection vs documented street violence gap.

WSM.name: Samoa
WSM.summary:
Samoa is Reduced Risk for trans visitors — anchored by one of the world's most institutionalized third-gender traditions. Fa'afafine (and fa'atama) are culturally embedded: recognized as heirs to customary land and eligible for matai (chiefly) titles within fa'a Sāmoa, organized nationally through the Samoa Fa'afafine Association (a formal UN UPR stakeholder since 1987), and visible through a famous pageant culture. Samoa repealed its colonial-era “female impersonation” crime in 2013, so no law touches gender expression itself.

The remaining negatives are modest for a visitor: no anti-discrimination law and no legal gender recognition (both resident-facing); documented discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against fa'afafine (APTN peer-led study — primarily resident/domestic contexts); isolated police-harassment reports (2 respondents, no convictions); and village fono councils that enforce conservative dress and behaviour norms. The unenforced sodomy statute is a situational risk for a fraction of visitors, not a trans-universal one.

Calibration (Aug 2026, two rounds of pairwise challenge): on traveler-facing axes Samoa beats Slovakia (0.69) on public presence, outing violence, and state climate; beats Greece (0.75) on public presence, police predation, and documented violence; and beats Romania (0.67) on every axis. It sits level with Greece — its lack of EU-style institutional recourse (a resident-weighted factor) is the only axis where European comparators hold an edge, and Estonia (0.77) keeps a 0.02 edge on that basis alone.
WSM.outOfScopeNotes: Fa\u2019afafine cultural embedding is informal protection; criminalisation unenforced.

TON.name: Tonga
TON.summary: Tonga is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. The Criminal Offences Act criminalises sodomy (10 years, plus corporal punishment on paper — unenforced in recent years) and also criminalises males “impersonating a female” while soliciting — a direct trans-expression statute on the books. Against that: Tonga has a visible leiti (trans-feminine) community with the famous Miss Galaxy pageant (documented by the Washington Post in 2024), family and church networks that are devout but not systematically violent, and no documented recent prosecutions. Pairwise: below Samoa (0.48 — stronger community organisation, no impersonation statute) and above Jordan (0.44).
TON.outOfScopeNotes: The male-impersonation statute is on the books but unenforced.

KIR.name: Kiribati
KIR.summary: Kiribati is High Risk. Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced); no LGR; tiny, isolated, church-dominated society with no visible community infrastructure. Pairwise: level with Kenya (0.38), below Tonga (0.46).

TUV.name: Tuvalu
TUV.summary: Tuvalu is Elevated Risk. Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced); no LGR; very small, tight-knit, church-centred society; no documented anti-trans violence (population ~11,000). Pairwise: above Kiribati (0.38 — comparable law, slightly less isolation-driven vulnerability) and below Tonga (0.46).

SLB.name: Solomon Islands
SLB.summary: Solomon Islands is High Risk. Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years); no LGR; documented social hostility; weak state capacity post-Tensions; no open community infrastructure. Pairwise: level with Sri Lanka (0.33), below Tuvalu (0.40), above Papua New Guinea (0.21).

VUT.name: Vanuatu
VUT.summary: Vanuatu is Elevated Risk. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised); no LGR; small VPride community in Port Vila; kastom and church conservatism but no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Pairwise: level with Trinidad & Tobago (0.42)/Rwanda (0.44) region, below Fiji (0.63) and above Solomon Islands (0.33).

NRU.name: Nauru
NRU.summary: Nauru is Elevated Risk. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2016; tiny population (~12,000); no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; the asylum-detention legacy shaped its international image but not its LGBT law. Pairwise: level with Paraguay (0.52), above Tuvalu (0.40).

PLW.name: Palau
PLW.summary: Palau is Elevated Risk. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2014; small, US-associated, tourism-dependent; no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence. Pairwise: level with Suriname (0.58), above Nauru (0.52).

FSM.name: Micronesia (FSM)
FSM.summary: The Federated States of Micronesia is Elevated Risk. No federal criminalisation (some states historically had provisions); US-associated; no LGR; no documented anti-trans pattern; very thin data. Pairwise: level with USA (0.50)/Mexico (0.50) by coincidence of profile (weak data, no hostility evidence), below Palau (0.58).

MHL.name: Marshall Islands
MHL.summary: The Marshall Islands is Elevated Risk. Same-sex conduct legal; US-associated; no LGR; no documented anti-trans pattern; very thin data. Pairwise: level with Nauru (0.52).

BEN.name: Benin
BEN.summary: Benin is High Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but 76crimes documents that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace; the Hirondelles Club provides safe housing for LGBT youth fleeing family violence. No LGR, no anti-discrimination law; community organises underground. Pairwise: below Sri Lanka (0.33) and above Jamaica (0.31).
BEN.outOfScopeNotes: Lynching pattern is documented climate, not statute.

TGO.name: Togo
TGO.summary: Togo is High Risk. The Penal Code criminalises “immodest or unnatural acts” (3 years); limited recent enforcement evidence but documented discrimination and violence; no LGR. Pairwise: below Azerbaijan (0.30) and above Malaysia (0.28).

NER.name: Niger
NER.summary: Niger is High Risk — and newly criminalising: in March 2025 the junta's Charter of Refoundation explicitly outlawed “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the first time (Article 25). Junta rule, jihadist insurgency, no recourse. Pairwise: level with Mali (0.19)/Nigeria (0.19) cluster, above Burkina Faso (0.22)? No — below BFA (0.22): Niger's explicit naming of LGBT people in the charter is more totalising than BFA's family-code provision.
NER.outOfScopeNotes: March 2025 criminalisation is brand new; enforcement undocumented.

TCD.name: Chad
TCD.summary: Chad is High Risk. Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2017 (misdemeanour, up to 2 years); junta-adjacent governance; no LGR; no community infrastructure; very thin data. Pairwise: level with Cameroon (0.21), above Niger (0.20).

GAB.name: Gabon
GAB.summary: Gabon is Elevated Risk — and on a surprising positive trajectory: after briefly criminalising same-sex intimacy in 2019, it decriminalised in 2020, and in November 2024 voters ratified a new constitution that rejected calls to criminalise homosexuality. No LGR; social conservatism; but the constitutional debate is now public and the pro-criminalisation side lost. Pairwise: level with USA/Mexico (0.50), above Côte d'Ivoire (0.34) — a stark intra-regional contrast — and below Paraguay (0.52).
GAB.outOfScopeNotes: 2020 decriminalisation + 2024 constitution are formal; social climate lags.

COG.name: Republic of the Congo
COG.summary: Republic of the Congo is High Risk. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised); EUAA COI (2024) documents societal discrimination, police harassment, and absence of protection; no LGR; small underground community. Pairwise: level with Lebanon/Kyrgyzstan (0.36), below Gabon (0.50) and above Côte d'Ivoire (0.34).

BDI.name: Burundi
BDI.summary: Burundi is Do Not Travel for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has been criminalised since 2009 (2 years), and the head of state himself has called for mob violence: in December 2023, President Ndayishimiye said LGBT people should be “taken to a stadium and stoned” because “that's what they deserve” — condemned by HRW as stoking fear; the Iteka League called it a call to lynching. There is no LGR, no community infrastructure (the oldest rights group works from exile), and arbitrary detention is routine. Pairwise: level with Tanzania (0.18), above Uganda (0.17 — death-penalty statute).
BDI.outOfScopeNotes: Presidential incitement is documented by HRW (Jan 2024).

CAF.name: Central African Republic
CAF.summary: Central African Republic is High Risk. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the state barely exists outside Bangui; armed groups control most territory; mob violence and police extortion against perceived LGBT people are documented; no LGR, no community infrastructure. Pairwise: level with Malawi (0.26), above Zambia (0.24), below Senegal (0.27).

GIN.name: Guinea
GIN.summary: Guinea is High Risk. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (3 years); a 2024 UPR stakeholder report documents violence and discrimination from both state and non-state actors; junta rule since 2021; no LGR. Pairwise: level with Senegal/Zimbabwe (0.27), below Sierra Leone-region peers.

LBR.name: Liberia
LBR.summary: Liberia is High Risk. Sodomy is criminalised (1 year, both sexes — a domestic-origin law, never colonised); a legislator is seeking support for a harsh 2024 anti-homosexuality bill (so far unsuccessful); mob violence is documented; no LGR. Pairwise: below Sri Lanka (0.33) and above Azerbaijan (0.30).
LBR.outOfScopeNotes: Active hostile bill (2024) not yet passed.

MDG.name: Madagascar
MDG.summary: Madagascar is Elevated Risk for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal — unusual for the region — but France 24 documents that LGBT people must hide to keep jobs and live in peace; there is no LGR, no anti-discrimination law, and no visible community outside Antananarivo. No documented police targeting pattern. Pairwise: above Armenia (0.46) and below Kenya (0.38)? No — above KEN (0.38: Madagascar has no criminalisation; Kenya does). Level with Turkey (0.47).
MDG.outOfScopeNotes: Thin data; legal but closeted profile.

COM.name: Comoros
COM.summary: Comoros is High Risk. The 2020 Penal Code criminalises acts “contrary to morality or against nature” (2 years), enforced: two women were detained in June 2024 after asking an Islamic preacher to marry them, convicted in December 2024 (released for time served). No LGR; small conservative archipelago. Pairwise: level with Malawi (0.26), above Zambia (0.24).
COM.outOfScopeNotes: 2024 prosecution is same-sex (climate); shows active enforcement.

DJI.name: Djibouti
DJI.summary: Djibouti is High Risk. The penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct, but vague “good morals” provisions (Arts 353/354) make homosexuality “de facto illegal” in practice; no anti-discrimination law, no LGR, no community infrastructure; authoritarian state with US/French bases but no rights space. Pairwise: level with Benin (0.32), above Benin's lynching documentation? — comparable; below Sri Lanka (0.33).

MRT.name: Mauritania
MRT.summary: Mauritania is Do Not Travel for trans visitors — one of the world's most dangerous legal environments. The 1983 Penal Code criminalises “acts against nature” with death by stoning (de facto moratorium on executions, but the statute is live); and Cairo 52 documents that gender nonconformity is effectively criminalised through debauchery, heresy, and Islamic-morality provisions — trans people can be apprehended solely for their gender expression. There is no LGR, no healthcare, no community, and sharia courts operate alongside the civil system. Pairwise: level with Syria/Yemen (0.06), above Somalia (0.04) and Afghanistan (0.02).

GNB.name: Guinea-Bissau
GNB.summary: Guinea-Bissau is Elevated Risk. Same-sex conduct is legal (one of few West African states never to criminalise); no LGR, no protections; chronic instability (coups) and weak state; documented social hostility but no mob-lynching pattern of Benin's type. Pairwise: level with Trinidad & Tobago (0.42), above Côte d'Ivoire (0.34).

GNQ.name: Equatorial Guinea
GNQ.summary: Equatorial Guinea is High Risk. The 2022 penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct — but a 2024 Synergía report documents twelve women imprisoned between January and August 2024 in police raids led by the Armed Forces and State Security, with detention-for-bribes and indefinite imprisonment; a Draft Law “Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals” (2020, status unclear) would formally criminalise. Africa's longest-ruling dictatorship; no recourse. Pairwise: above Egypt (0.22) and below Ghana (0.24).
GNQ.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 documented prisonings targeted lesbians; trans people face the same machinery via gender-nonconformity.

SWZ.name: Eswatini
SWZ.summary: Eswatini is High Risk for trans visitors. Common law criminalises same-sex intimacy; trans people have no access to LGR and limited healthcare; the absolute monarchy punishes dissent harshly (sedition laws; activists assassinated, per BTI 2024); LGBT people face documented discrimination. Eswatini Pride has proceeded annually since 2018 under heavy conditions — a small space of visibility. Pairwise: level with Kenya/Georgia (0.38), below Rwanda (0.44).
SWZ.outOfScopeNotes: Monarchy repression is general; Pride proceeds annually.

LSO.name: Lesotho
LSO.summary: Lesotho is Elevated Risk. Same-sex conduct is legal (sodomy common-law crime struck down in 2012); the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho documents failures to prevent violence, harassment and discrimination by state and non-state actors (2024 UPR submission); no LGR; small organised community inside South Africa's geographic envelope. Pairwise: below Madagascar (0.47) and above Rwanda (0.44).

CPV.name: Cabo Verde
CPV.summary: Cabo Verde is Reduced Risk — Africa's most tolerant jurisdiction alongside South Africa's legal tier. Same-sex relations are legal; employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; Praia and Mindelo host visible Pride events; the culture is notably relaxed by regional standards. No explicit GI protections and no LGR statute (administrative practice unclear), but no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Pairwise: above Romania (0.67) and below Botswana (0.65)? — no, above BWA (0.65): Cabo Verde's social acceptance outperforms Botswana's litigation-dependent path. Level with Slovakia (0.69)/Hungary (0.68) region.
CPV.outOfScopeNotes: LGR statute absent; evidence base thin but consistent.

Pairwise: level with Malaysia/Tajikistan (0.28), above Senegal (0.27), below Azerbaijan (0.30).
